comparison: Strong agreement on temporal progression of velocity deficits (C6, C7, C30, C31, C66-C73, C96-C97). Both recognize immediate deficits followed by progressive decline. OpenEval provides detailed statistical support while peer reviewers emphasize the dual mechanism insight as a key contribution.

Both support velocity reduction findings (C3-C5, C25, C41-C44, C99). OpenEval provides comprehensive statistical analysis across multiple claim groups. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm the finding is 'convincingly demonstrated' with target-specific effects.

Both address muscle torque deficits (C4, C27, C50-C55). OpenEval integrates torque findings with broader kinematic analysis. Peer reviewers specifically highlight the inverse dynamics modeling as extending previous work.

Strong agreement on correlation between velocity reduction and coupling torques (C57-C61, C128-C129). Both recognize the dual mechanism: correlation with coupling torques plus additional velocity reduction in low-coupling movements. OpenEval notes mechanistic interpretation is inferential.

Both support increased motor noise/decomposition findings (C8, C32, C80-C85, C90-C91, C98, C138). OpenEval emphasizes velocity-matching approach as strong evidence. Peer reviewers explicitly confirm decomposition occurs even when velocities are matched to controls.

Both address trajectory variability (C86, C88-C89, C98, C139-C140). OpenEval provides statistical support (p<0.001) and notes persistence across trials. Peer reviewers confirm increased variance even with velocity matching.

Both support the dual mechanism interpretation (C9, C34-C37, C126-C127, C145). OpenEval treats these as high-level integrative claims. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse the dual mechanism as 'convincingly demonstrated' and 'clarifying.'

Both support HFS methodology (C22-C24, C93, C151-C154). OpenEval notes validation against patient deficits while acknowledging limitations. Peer reviewers praise HFS as 'an important advance' with 'attractive' temporal resolution.

Both address within-trial vs out-of-trial movement comparison (C46-C47). OpenEval provides statistical support and notes mechanistic explanation is inferential. Peer reviewers accept this finding as part of broader velocity reduction results without specific challenge.

Both rate asymmetry explanation as uncertain (C130, C135-C136). OpenEval notes data don't definitively distinguish between mechanisms. Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'it is still not entirely clear why disruption...is not seen for inward targets' despite potential explanations.

Both acknowledge HFS limitations (C156, C158, C162). OpenEval notes uncertainty about extent and specificity of block. Peer reviewers accept these acknowledged limitations don't undermine validity of the approach.

Partial overlap on temporal resolution advantages (C127, C147). OpenEval supports these as summary claims. Peer reviewers explicitly praise temporal resolution as key strength enabling differentiation of acute vs sub-acute effects.
OpenEval addresses basic behavioral outcomes (C38-C40) as part of comprehensive kinematic analysis. Peer reviewers don't specifically discuss these claims but accept overall experimental results.

OpenEval rates motor noise mechanism as uncertain (C141-C146, including C145-C146) due to speculative internal model interpretation. Peer reviewers support the dual mechanism broadly (including C145-C146) as convincingly demonstrated, focusing on empirical findings rather than theoretical mechanism.
OpenEval supports literature contextualization claims (C100-C105, C107) including compensatory hypothesis. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation of these literature integration claims.
OpenEval supports integration with historical literature on acute cerebellar injury (C108-C116, C121-C122). No corresponding specific peer review evaluation of these historical context claims.
OpenEval supports reasoning about alternative mechanisms for torque reduction (C118-C120). No corresponding peer review evaluation of this specific mechanistic reasoning.
OpenEval supports background and motivation claims (C1-C2, C11-C21, C92, C125) as accurately representing prior literature. No corresponding specific peer review evaluation of background claims.
OpenEval supports basic biomechanical principles (C48-C49) as established knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation of these foundational claims.
OpenEval supports methodological details about subjects and ethics (C149-C150). No corresponding peer review evaluation of these procedural claims.
